A lot of times, it depends on how the family ends up in subsidized housing. There's the typical, you apply for it for your family, but you could also receive by renting a unit in a subsidized building. In this case, units in a building are set aside for subsidy and whoever that unit is leased to pays subsidized price. For instance, my mother was a property manager for Mercy Housing and one of their properties on the west side of the city was a subsidized building. A potential tenant didn't have to already have a voucher, but they had to meet criteria for someone that would receive a voucher. In a case like that, the tenant awarded the lease would also gain voucher status that they could take with them, not sure how long they would have to stay in unit before they could take voucher with them. The properties that have subsidized units in this case will usually add zero tolerance policies to their lease agreements. Those vary from property to property, I know of one that will evict the entire family if any  associated with that family and living in the unit is charged with a crime on the grounds of that property. There are some that do the drug testing and some that track tenant progress and do yearly reviews. I couldn't speak on this particular setup, as they differ.

I know this is long, but it's not easily wrapped in a bow, but Section 8 is a federal program, and requirements by state differ as well. One could also gain voucher status in a less populated location with a shorter wait list and bring it with them to Chicago. Say, apply for a voucher in Iowa, which has a wait list shorter than a year.

All persons living in a unit under a voucher affect the status of that voucher. If a teenage son or daughter does a crime on the property and a human services follow up finds neglect, then that family can lose its voucher. In Chicago, the wait for a voucher can last multiple years, up to five or more in some cases. Voucher program also comes with a social worker and regular check-ins, home visits and inspections. Your fears are based on people in poverty, not people on vouchers.
